Pathology-02.question: ২১) Tuberculoid leprosy
২২) Most important mode of transmission in lepromatous leprosy
২৩) Smallest free living organism
২৪) Which one remains positive for life in syphilis?
Pathology-02.exp:
TPHA (Treponema pallidum Hemagglutination Assay) is a treponemal test that usually remains positive for life, even after adequate treatment. Therefore, it is not useful for monitoring treatment response.

Why other options are incorrect:

  • VDRL: Non-treponemal test; titers decrease after treatment and may become negative.

  • RPR: Non-treponemal test; used to monitor disease activity and response to therapy.

  • FTA-ABS: A treponemal test that also often remains positive for life, Exam Pearl:
    Treponemal tests (TPHA, FTA-ABS) stay positive for life; non-treponemal tests (VDRL, RPR) are used to monitor treatment response.but in single-best-answer MCQs TPHA is the standard answer.

Pathology-02.option4: Suppression of antibody response to new antigen
Pathology-02.exp:
Protein-energy malnutrition (PEM) causes both cell-mediated and humoral immune dysfunction. A characteristic defect is the poor antibody response to new antigens because of impaired T-cell help and B-cell function. However, antibody levels to previously encountered antigens are often relatively preserved.

Why other options are incorrect:

  • Transient suppression of delayed hypersensitivity: This is classically seen in measles, not malnutrition.

  • Killing of helper T cell: Characteristic of HIV infection.

  • Reduced synthesis of IgG: Total IgG is often normal or only mildly affected; the key defect is the reduced response to new antigens.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

Condition Main immune defect
Malnutrition (PEM) Poor antibody response to new antigens + impaired cell-mediated immunity
Measles Transient suppression of delayed hypersensitivity
HIV/AIDS CD4⁺ helper T-cell destruction
Bruton agammaglobulinemia Absent B cells, markedly ↓ immunoglobulins

Exam Pearl:
Protein-energy malnutrition → Thymic atrophy, impaired T-cell function, and poor antibody response to newly encountered antigens, increasing susceptibility to infections.

Pathology-02.question: ৪১) “Break-bone fever” is suggestive of?
Pathology-02.exp:
"Break-bone fever" is the classic nickname for dengue fever because of the severe muscle and joint pain (myalgia and arthralgia) experienced by patients, making them feel as if their bones are breaking.

Clinical features include:

  • High fever

  • Severe headache

  • Retro-orbital pain

  • Severe myalgia and arthralgia ("break-bone pain")

  • Maculopapular rash

  • Thrombocytopenia and, in severe cases, dengue hemorrhagic fever/shock syndrome

Why other options are incorrect:

  • Lyme disease: Caused by Borrelia burgdorferi; presents with erythema migrans and arthritis.

  • Relapsing fever: Caused by Borrelia recurrentis; characterized by recurrent febrile episodes.

  • Typhoid fever: Caused by Salmonella Typhi; presents with prolonged fever, abdominal symptoms, and rose spots.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

Disease Characteristic feature
Dengue fever "Break-bone fever", severe myalgia/arthralgia
Lyme disease Erythema migrans ("bull's-eye" rash)
Relapsing fever Recurrent fever episodes
Typhoid fever Step-ladder fever, rose spots

Exam Pearl:
"Break-bone fever" = Dengue fever (Flavivirus) transmitted by Aedes aegypti mosquito.

Pathology-02.question: ৪২) Which of the following is the commonest physical finding in enteric fever?
Pathology-02.exp:
In enteric (typhoid) fever, the commonest physical finding is a coated tongue (often described as a white-coated tongue with a clean red tip and margins). Other common findings include fever, relative bradycardia (Faget sign), abdominal discomfort, hepatosplenomegaly, and occasionally rose spots.

Why other options are incorrect:

  • Abdominal tenderness: May occur but is not the commonest physical finding.

  • Rose spots: Characteristic but seen in only a minority of patients (about 10–30%).

  • Hepatosplenomegaly: Can occur but is less common than a coated tongue.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

Feature Enteric (Typhoid) fever
Commonest physical finding Coated tongue
Characteristic rash Rose spots
Causative organism Salmonella Typhi
Relative bradycardia Faget sign
Carrier state Gallbladder

Exam Pearl:
Typhoid fever → Coated tongue is the commonest physical finding; chronic carriers usually harbor Salmonella Typhi in the gallbladder.

Pathology-02.question: ৪৩) Which of the following is not a presentation of tertiary syphilis ?
Pathology-02.exp:
Condylomata lata are broad, flat, moist, highly infectious lesions that occur during secondary syphilis, not tertiary syphilis.

Tertiary syphilis (years after untreated infection) is characterized by:

  • Gummatous syphilis (gumma)

  • Cardiovascular syphilis (especially ascending aortic aneurysm and aortic regurgitation)

  • Neurosyphilis (tabes dorsalis, general paresis, symptomatic neurosyphilis)

Why other options are correct:

  • Gumma: Classic feature of tertiary syphilis.

  • Cardiovascular syphilis: Occurs in tertiary disease.

  • Symptomatic neurosyphilis: A manifestation of tertiary syphilis.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

Stage Characteristic features
Primary Painless chancre
Secondary Condylomata lata, generalized rash (including palms/soles), lymphadenopathy
Latent Asymptomatic
Tertiary Gumma, cardiovascular syphilis, neurosyphilis

Exam Pearl:
Condylomata lata = Secondary syphilis; Gumma + Aortitis + Neurosyphilis = Tertiary syphilis.

Pathology-02.question: ৪৪) For the diagnosis of primary pulmonary tuberculosis in children, who often do not expectorate sputum, specimen for culture can be obtained from?
Pathology-02.exp:
Children with primary pulmonary tuberculosis usually cannot expectorate sputum. Overnight, they swallow respiratory secretions containing Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Therefore, early-morning gastric lavage (gastric aspirate) is collected before the child eats to recover the swallowed bacilli for smear microscopy, culture, or molecular tests (e.g., GeneXpert MTB/RIF).

Why other options are incorrect:

  • Nasal secretion: Not suitable for diagnosing pulmonary TB.

  • Throat swab: Low diagnostic yield for M. tuberculosis.

  • Faeces: Not the standard specimen for pulmonary TB diagnosis.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

Patient Preferred specimen
Adult with pulmonary TB Sputum
Young child unable to produce sputum Early-morning gastric lavage (gastric aspirate)
Alternative Induced sputum / Bronchoalveolar lavage (selected cases)

Exam Pearl:
In children suspected of pulmonary TB who cannot produce sputum, the specimen of choice is an early-morning gastric aspirate (gastric lavage).

Pathology-02.question: ৪৫) Which of the following is not a characteristic of rabies virus?
Pathology-02.exp:
Rabies virus belongs to the Rhabdoviridae family (Lyssavirus genus). It is:

  • Bullet-shaped

  • Enveloped

  • Single-stranded RNA virus

  • Negative-sense (negative-polarity) RNA virus, not positive-sense.

Therefore, "Positive polarity" is not a characteristic of the rabies virus.

Why other options are correct:

  • Bullet shaped: Classical morphology of rabies virus.

  • Enveloped: Yes.

  • Exam Pearl:
    Rabies = Bullet-shaped, enveloped, negative-sense ssRNA virus with Negri bodies in neurons.

    Single-stranded RNA: Yes, it is a (-) ssRNA virus.

Pathology-02.question: ৪৬) Leptospirainterrogans persist indefinitely in
Pathology-02.exp:
Leptospira interrogans persists in the renal proximal convoluted tubules, especially in reservoir animals (e.g., rats, dogs, cattle). The organisms are shed in urine for prolonged periods, which is the major source of transmission to humans through contaminated water or soil.

Why other options are incorrect:

  • Mucous membrane: Portal of entry, not the site of persistent colonization.

  • Bowman's capsule: Not the site where Leptospira persists.

  • Juxtaglomerular apparatus: Not involved in chronic colonization.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

Feature Leptospira interrogans
Organism Spirochete
Reservoir Rats, dogs, cattle
Site of persistence Proximal convoluted tubules of kidney
Route of transmission Contact with urine-contaminated water/soil
Severe disease Weil's disease (jaundice, renal failure, hemorrhage)

Exam Pearl:
Leptospira persists in the renal proximal convoluted tubules and is excreted in urine, facilitating transmission.

Pathology-02.question: ৪৮) Listeria causes more significant infection in all of the following except
Pathology-02.exp:
Listeria monocytogenes causes particularly severe disease in:

  • Immunocompromised patients

  • Pregnant women

  • Neonates

These are the classic high-risk groups emphasized in microbiology exams. Although older adults are also at increased risk of invasive listeriosis, in traditional single-best-answer MBBS MCQs the first three are considered the principal risk groups, making "Older adults" the expected EXCEPT answer.

Why other options are incorrect:

  • Immunocompromised: High risk for septicemia and meningitis.

  • Pregnant women: May develop mild illness but can transmit infection to the fetus, causing miscarriage, stillbirth, or neonatal sepsis.

  • Neonate: High risk for septicemia and meningitis.

  • Older adults: Increased risk exists, but this is the least appropriate option among the choices in the context of this exam question.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

High-risk group Common manifestation
Pregnant women Fetal infection, abortion, stillbirth
Neonates Sepsis, meningitis
Immunocompromised Septicemia, meningitis
Older adults Increased risk, especially invasive disease

Exam Pearl:
Listeria = Intracellular Gram-positive rod + transmitted via unpasteurized dairy/ready-to-eat foods + classically affects pregnant women, neonates, and immunocompromised patients.

Pathology-02.question: ৪৯) Infections that can be used as bioterrorism
Pathology-02.exp:
Bacillus anthracis is the causative organism of anthrax and is a well-known Category A bioterrorism agent because its spores are highly resistant, can be aerosolized, and may cause severe inhalational anthrax with high mortality if untreated.

Why other options are incorrect:

  • Melioidosis (Burkholderia pseudomallei): Can cause severe disease but is not the classic answer in standard MBBS bioterrorism MCQs.

  • Nocardiosis (Nocardia): Opportunistic infection in immunocompromised patients; not a recognized classic bioterrorism agent.

  • Actinomyces: Causes chronic suppurative infections (actinomycosis); not used as a bioterrorism agent.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

Organism Importance
Bacillus anthracis Anthrax; Category A bioterrorism agent
Yersinia pestis Plague; Category A agent
Francisella tularensis Tularemia; Category A agent
Clostridium botulinum toxin Botulism; Category A agent

Exam Pearl:
Classic bioterrorism organisms: Anthrax (Bacillus anthracis), Plague (Yersinia pestis), Tularemia (Francisella tularensis), Botulinum toxin, Smallpox virus.

Pathology-02.question: ৫০) Mycobacterium leprae has tropism for
Pathology-02.exp:
Mycobacterium leprae has a marked tropism for Schwann cells of the peripheral nervous system. Infection of these cells leads to:

  • Peripheral neuropathy

  • Loss of sensation

  • Muscle weakness

  • Nerve thickening and deformities

The organism prefers cooler areas of the body, such as the skin, peripheral nerves, nose, ears, and testes.

Why other options are incorrect:

  • Extraglomerular mesangial cells: Not a target of M. leprae.

  • Upper respiratory mucosae: Important site of entry and shedding, but the characteristic tissue tropism is for Schwann cells.

  • Testes: May be involved in lepromatous leprosy, but not the primary tropism.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

Organism Tissue tropism
Mycobacterium leprae Schwann cells (peripheral nerves)
Clinical effect Peripheral neuropathy, anesthesia, nerve thickening
Preferred temperature Cooler parts of the body

Exam Pearl:
The hallmark of leprosy is infection of Schwann cells, resulting in peripheral nerve damage and sensory loss.
